passage: Good morning and welcome to Hartwell House. I'm Patrick, and I'll be your guide for the next hour. Before we start, a few practical points. From there we go upstairs to the library, which holds nine thousand volumes, and we finish in the walled garden. If the weather turns, we will visit the stables instead of the garden. passage: Today we turn to the urban heat island effect, the observation that cities are consistently warmer than the countryside around them. In very large cities the difference can reach seven degrees Celsius at night, though two to three degrees is far more typical. Three mechanisms explain most of this. First, materials. Concrete and asphalt absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly after sunset, which is why the gap is largest at night rather than at noon, as students often assume. Second, geometry. Tall buildings form narrow canyons that trap heat and block the open sky, reducing the rate at which surfaces can cool. Third, waste heat from vehicles, factories and above all air conditioning. Note the feedback here: hotter cities use more air conditioning, which pushes still more heat outdoors. Vegetation is the single most effective remedy, because trees both shade surfaces and cool the air through evaporation. Reflective, light coloured roofs help too, but only where they are widely adopted.

Why concrete is used in modern buildings
How trees are planted in city centres

passage: In this lecture I want to look at the relationship between sleep and memory. The traditional view was that sleep simply gives the brain a rest. Evidence from the last thirty years suggests something far more active: during sleep the brain replays and reorganises the day's experiences. In one well known experiment, participants learned a list of word pairs and were tested twelve hours later. Those who slept in between recalled roughly forty per cent more than those who stayed awake. Forty, not fourteen, which is the figure sometimes misquoted. Different stages seem to matter for different kinds of learning. Deep slow wave sleep, concentrated in the first half of the night, appears to support factual memory, while REM sleep, which dominates the second half, is linked to skills and to creative problem solving. This has a practical consequence. Cutting your night short by two hours does not remove a fixed slice of sleep; it removes most of your REM. So a student who revises facts all night may keep the facts and lose the flexibility to use them.

So a student who revises facts all night may keep the facts and lose the flexibility to use them.
